claims.text: Near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles with minimized lattice strain from atomic-radius mismatch will resist diffusion-driven elemental segregation better during high-temperature service than nanoparticles with larger mismatches.

Near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles with minimized lattice strain will resist surface oxidation better during high-temperature service than nanoparticles with larger atomic-radius mismatches.
The initial nanoparticles exhibit significant atomic disorder.
Differences in constituent atomic radii produce notable lattice strain in the initial nanoparticles.
Substituting constituents with elements having closer atomic radii will reduce overall lattice strain.
Reducing atomic-size mismatch will modify local atomic ordering.
Reducing lattice strain decreases the activation energy for atomic diffusion at high temperature.
A decrease in the activation energy for atomic diffusion limits diffusion-driven elemental segregation and surface oxidation.
Limiting diffusion preserves the disordered solid-solution state.
Preserving the disordered solid-solution state maintains structural integrity and chemical uniformity during service.
Strain-modified nanoparticles will segregate more slowly than the baseline nanoparticles.
Strain-modified nanoparticles will oxidize more slowly than the baseline nanoparticles.
Reduced segregation and oxidation will improve structural and chemical stability.
The modified nanoparticles will retain catalytic activity or thermoelectric efficiency better over time than the baseline nanoparticles.
Larger atomic-radius mismatches produce higher lattice strain in the baseline nanoparticles.
Higher lattice strain enhances atomic diffusion at elevated temperatures.
The proposed strain-controlled mechanism applies throughout catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K.
Reactive-gas partial pressures can modulate the effects of atomic-radius mismatch on diffusion and phase stability.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and baseline associate lower strain with slower diffusion and higher strain with enhanced diffusion, but the mechanism says lower strain decreases the diffusion activation energy. Within an activated-diffusion account, a lower activation barrier would imply easier or faster diffusion, so the stated causal sign is internally inconsistent.

The intervention changes one or more constituent elements, whereas the boundary condition says overall composition is held constant and strain is the only major difference. Elemental substitution necessarily changes chemical identity and may alter oxidation, diffusion, phase energetics, and functionality independently of strain.
